rv.q: Rebecca Frecknall’s new revival of Kander and Ebb’s musical set in interwar Berlin is a stunning, breathlessly exciting theatrical happening.
At the end of the year, Rebecca Frecknall's production of Cabaret stands revealed as 2021's kill-for-a-ticket theatrical triumph.
It may be a little parsimonious in its pleasures, but this eagerly anticipated new staging of Cabaret certainly looks good, sounds good – and runs like clockwork.
If this show is sold on his star turn, we get more than our money’s worth with his blinding performance – in this blinder of a show.
Liza Sadovy's doomed romance with Elliot Levey's Jewish lodger, Herr Schultz, comes close to eclipsing Sally and Cliff.
Cabaret looks terrific, sounds pretty good and retains its powerful "live and let live" message.
The whole production is about as good as theatre gets; with every shade of emotion and absolutely no wasted dialogue or scene.
The Kit Kat Club is the ultimate escape.
Perhaps the best musical-theatre performance I have ever seen live is Buckley's rendition of the title song.
It tricks us into feeling as if we’re at a party when really we’re at the most visceral display of political theatre in the West End.
That one moment, the shattering of those small but universal dreams, tells us everything we need to know.
But fundamentally, it’s a production of Cabaret that’s good enough to triumph over the myriad distractions it throws in its own path.
This is an experience well up to the standards of the very best you'd pay a lot for at Glyndebourne or the Royal Opera.
